misconceptions.description: Treating an AI-text-detector percentage as proof that a student cheated
misconceptions.trigger: teacher issues an academic-integrity consequence based on a detector score alone
misconceptions.feedback: AI detectors produce probabilistic guesses with documented false positives, especially for multilingual and neurodivergent writers. Use process evidence, drafts, and a conversation, not a percentage, to make an integrity judgment.

misconceptions.description: Assuming every use of generative AI on student work is academic dishonesty regardless of the assignment's allowed use
misconceptions.trigger: teacher penalizes brainstorming or grammar help that the assignment permitted
misconceptions.feedback: Define allowed, assisted, and prohibited uses for the specific assignment before judging. Cheating is doing what the task forbade, not using a tool the task allowed.

misconceptions.description: Assessing only the polished final text, which makes generative-AI shortcuts invisible and unteachable
misconceptions.trigger: teacher collects only the finished essay with no drafts, notes, or process artifacts
misconceptions.feedback: Collect process evidence: outlines, annotated drafts, and a short reflection on what AI did and did not do. Process makes both learning and shortcuts visible.

misconceptions.description: Reading polished AI-assisted prose as evidence that the student understands the content
misconceptions.trigger: teacher assigns a high grade to fluent work without checking for the student's own reasoning
misconceptions.feedback: Generative AI produces fluent text without comprehension. Probe with a quick oral question or an in-class write to see whether the student can reconstruct the reasoning.
